title: The highest-fiber legumes: a practical nutrition ranking

seo.title: Highest-fiber legumes: beans, lentils and chickpeas ranked
seo.meta_description: Beans, lentils and chickpeas are all rich in fiber when cooked. Compare fiber per 100 g and per realistic serving to see which differences matter.
seo.search_intent: Compare the fiber content of common cooked legumes and understand how much a normal serving contributes.

excerpt: Most cooked beans provide roughly 7–10 g of fiber per 100 g, while lentils and chickpeas are commonly around 7–8 g. A 1-cup serving can easily deliver about 12–19 g of fiber, so eating legumes regularly matters more than chasing a tiny difference between varieties.
content_html:
Legume rankings become misleading fast when dry beans are compared with cooked lentils. Cooking adds a large amount of water, so nutrients become less concentrated per 100 g even though they have not simply vanished.

For a useful plate-level comparison, the fairest starting point is cooked, drained legumes.

Fiber in common cooked legumes

The figures below are approximate and can shift with variety and cooking method.

Cooked legumeFiber/100 gFiber in about 1 cup
Navy beans~10 g~19 g
Pinto beans~9 g~15 g
Black beans~8.7 g~15 g
Lentils~7.9 g~16 g
Chickpeas~7.6 g~12–13 g
Split peas~8.3 g~16 g

The useful takeaway is not that one bean wins by a gram or two. It is that a normal bowl of legumes can supply a very large share of a day's fiber.

Why dry-legume numbers look so much higher

Dry lentils and beans contain little water. After cooking, they absorb water and weigh much more. Fiber and protein are therefore spread across a larger cooked weight, which lowers the value per 100 g without implying a comparable nutrient loss.

Does first place matter?

If one cup of beans provides roughly 15–19 g of fiber and chickpeas provide around 12–13 g, there is a difference, but it is much smaller than the difference between eating legumes and skipping them entirely.

U.S. reference intakes vary by age and sex; for many adults they fall roughly in the 25–38 g per day range. A generous serving of legumes can therefore cover a substantial part of a day's fiber.

Fiber comes with protein too

Legumes are not isolated fiber supplements. One cup of cooked lentils provides roughly 18 g of protein along with folate, iron and complex carbohydrates. One cup of cooked chickpeas provides about 14–15 g of protein, plus roughly 12–13 g of fiber and a range of minerals.

That combination of fiber, protein, water and starch helps explain why legumes tend to be filling.

Canned beans still count

Canned legumes remain a useful source of fiber. Rinsing them can lower some of the sodium in the packing liquid without washing away the structural fiber inside the bean.

Cooking method and the liquid you keep or discard can shift the final numbers slightly, but the broad pattern is stable: lentils, beans, chickpeas, and split peas are all meaningful fiber sources. The exact winner can change with variety, water absorption, and database entry. That is why it is more useful to think in ranges than to treat a one-gram difference per 100 grams as a nutritional gap.

A normal bowl also puts the ranking into perspective. Eating 150 to 200 grams of cooked legumes can provide a substantial share of the day’s fiber while also adding starch, plant protein, potassium, folate, and iron. A food does not need to sit at the top of the table to make a practical difference if the portion is realistic and appears regularly.

Tolerance matters because increasing legumes quickly can cause bloating in people who are not used to much fermentable fiber. Starting with smaller portions, rinsing canned beans, chewing well, and increasing intake gradually can make the change easier. Drinking enough fluid also matters when total fiber rises.

The most useful strategy is variety across the week. Lentils cook quickly, chickpeas work well in salads and hummus, black or kidney beans suit stews and bowls, and split peas make thick soups. Rotating them gives similar fiber benefits with different textures, flavors, and micronutrient profiles.

Meal preparation can make legumes easier to use often. Cooking a large batch and freezing portions, or keeping a few no-salt-added cans in the pantry, removes much of the time barrier. A serving added to soup, salad, tacos, pasta sauce, or a grain bowl can raise fiber without turning every meal into a bean-based dish.

Fiber targets are easier to reach when legumes are combined with whole grains, vegetables, fruit, nuts, and seeds rather than expected to do all the work. That broader pattern also spreads different fermentable fibers across the diet, which can support a more varied gut microbiota.

The practical answer

If maximum concentration is your only criterion, several beans sit near the top. In everyday eating, however, beans, lentils and chickpeas are close enough that serving size, frequency and variety matter more than a narrow ranking.

faq.question: Which legumes have the most fiber?
faq.answer: Several cooked beans provide around 8–10 g of fiber per 100 g, with lentils and chickpeas close behind at roughly 7–8 g.

faq.question: How much fiber is in a cup of legumes?
faq.answer: Depending on the legume, a cup commonly provides about 12–19 g of fiber.

faq.question: Do canned beans still have fiber?
faq.answer: Yes. Canned beans remain fiber-rich, and rinsing them mainly helps reduce sodium rather than fiber.
